Scope

What this is (not) about

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk04 / 88

Briefing

Checklists were not invented by careful people.

They were invented after a crash.

On 30 October 1935 the Boeing Model 299 — the B-17 prototype — crashed on take-off at Wright Field because the gust locks were still engaged. The crew were among the best pilots in the country. The aircraft was simply more complex than memory could hold. The answer was not better pilots. The answer was the checklist.

✚

Your NOTAM package

The Changelog

Read before every flight. Not once, not sometimes. Every flight.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk12 / 88

Changelog

What a NOTAM actually is

  • A NOTAM — Notice to Air Missions — tells a crew what changed since last time.
  • Runway 07 closed. Navaid out of service. New obstacle 1.2 NM short of threshold.
  • It is not interesting reading. It is mandatory reading.
  • No crew departs on the assumption that the airport is the same as last month.

Yet we routinely upgrade TYPO3 on exactly that assumption.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk13 / 88

Changelog

Four types, four different demands

Breaking

Runway closed

Something was removed or changed incompatibly.

Fix before you can run on the new version. No grace period.

Deprecation

Airworthiness Directive with a compliance date

Still works — and is already scheduled for removal.

Fix now, on your schedule, or it becomes a Breaking change later.

Feature

New equipment fitted

New API or capability you may adopt.

Optional — but often the migration target of a deprecation.

Important

Operational bulletin

Behaviour changed in a way you should know about.

Read it. It is where the surprises hide.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk16 / 88

The one thing to remember

Today's Deprecation is tomorrow's Breaking change.

Deprecated in 12.0 → removed in 13.0. The changelog told you two years in advance.

This is why deprecation is not a phase-1 task. It is checked in all three phases, for three different reasons.

Changelog

Deprecation is checked in every phase

1Pre-Flight

Which deprecations of my CURRENT version am I still using?

They are the removals of the version you are flying to. Clear them while the old version still runs and still forgives you.

Extension Scanner · rector --dry-run

2Flight

Which of them actually bite now that they are gone?

What was a warning yesterday is a fatal error today. The scanner now ships the target version's rules.

Extension Scanner (v13 rules) · rector · fractor

3Post-Flight

Which NEW deprecations did I just inherit?

The version you just landed on deprecates things too. That list is the flight plan for the next upgrade.

Deprecation log · Extension Scanner · rector, next level set

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk21 / 88

Phase 1

How a crew starts the day

  • Dispatch prepares a flight information package before the crew ever reaches the aircraft.
  • Route, weather, NOTAMs, fuel, alternates, payload, and the MEL are already on paper.
  • The crew verifies it — they do not invent it at the gate.
  • Then they walk around the aircraft and look at it with their own eyes.

Nobody improvises a departure. The improvisation budget is saved for the things that actually go wrong.

Phase 1

Know your aircraft

You cannot plan a flight for an aircraft you have not inventoried.

# What am I actually running?
./vendor/bin/typo3 --version
composer show typo3/cms-core
php --version && composer show | wc -l

# What is installed, and what of it is mine?
./vendor/bin/typo3 extension:list
composer show --direct

# What is abandoned, outdated, or about to become someone else's problem?
composer outdated --direct
composer audit
  • Write the answers down. This is the aircraft you are flying, not the one you remember.
  • Every extension is one of four things: maintained, adoptable, replaceable, or a reason not to depart.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk27 / 88

Phase 1 · Tooling

Strong and weak matches

strong

6 findings

The scanner resolved the type and is certain. A definite usage of deprecated or removed API.

Fix it. This will break.

weak

7 findings

The name matches, but the type could not be resolved — $obj->getTreeList() might be TYPO3's, or might be entirely yours.

Verify by hand. Then decide, and record the decision.

The detection approach — based on static code analysis — is limited by concept: false positives/negatives are impossible to avoid.— the Extension Scanner, about itself

A weak match is not noise. It is an item you have not decided about yet.

From finding to changelog in one click

A strong match, expanded — TYPO3 12.4.45

  • The exact line: 39: 'signal' => BackendUtility::getUpdateSignalCode(),
  • The exact entry: Deprecation #96136, shipped in 12.0.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk29 / 88

Phase 1 · Tooling

Where the scanner stops

It only reads PHP

TypoScript, Fluid, TCA, YAML, FlexForms and .htaccess are never looked at.

It does not have a rule for everything

QueryBuilder->execute() has been deprecated since 12.0 — and has no scanner rule at all.

It cannot resolve dynamic code

String class names, variable method calls, and $GLOBALS juggling stay invisible.

It scans code, not behaviour

Changed defaults and changed rendering do not appear in any static scan.

This is not a flaw. It is one layer of defence — which is exactly why you add more.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk31 / 88

Phase 1 · Tooling

Make the aircraft stay clean

A scan you run once is a snapshot. A scan in CI is a standard.

# .gitlab-ci.yml
extension-scanner:
  stage: qa
  script:
    - composer install --no-progress
    - ./vendor/bin/typo3 extension:scan --all --no-progress
  # exits non-zero on strong matches -> the pipeline fails

# Checkstyle output for the merge-request annotations
    - ./vendor/bin/typo3 extension:scan --all --format=checkstyle > scan.xml
  artifacts:
    reports:
      codequality: scan.xml
  • New deprecated usage never gets merged in the first place.
  • The next upgrade then starts from zero instead of from archaeology.
Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk32 / 88

Phase 1 · Tooling

TCA is migrated behind your back

  • On every single request, TYPO3 rewrites outdated TCA in memory before anything uses it.
  • Your old configuration keeps working — so nothing ever tells you it is old.
  • TcaFactory::migrateTca() raises a single E_USER_DEPRECATED carrying the full list of what it changed.
  • In production that goes into the deprecation log, if you enabled it. Usually nobody looks.

This is the autopilot quietly trimming out an imbalance. The aircraft flies straight — right up until the day the autopilot is removed.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk33 / 88

Phase 1 · Tooling

“…these migrations will be removed.”

The core says it out loud, on every request, in the deprecation it raises. An auto-migration is not a fix. It is an Airworthiness Directive with an open deadline.

Verbatim from TcaFactory: “Automatic TCA migration done during bootstrap. Please adapt TCA accordingly, these migrations will be removed. The backend module ‘Configuration → TCA’ shows the modified values.”

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk42 / 88

Phase 1

The MEL — what you accept as broken

  • Aviation has a legal list of equipment that may be inoperative while the aircraft still dispatches.
  • Every item carries a condition, a procedure, and a rectification deadline.
  • You will not fix every finding before departure. That is normal and professional.
  • What is not professional is not writing down which ones you skipped, and why.

An undocumented accepted finding is not accepted. It is forgotten — and it will be rediscovered at the worst possible moment.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk43 / 88

Phase 1

Tests are your instruments

  • Clicking through the site is VFR — fine in daylight, useless at night and in cloud.
  • A functional test boots an actual TYPO3 and runs your code against the real core.
  • That is the difference: every other tool in this talk READS your code. Tests RUN it.
  • No tests? Then a smoke checklist before you depart — not after it breaks.

Instruments do not stop turbulence. They tell you which way is up while it happens.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk44 / 88

Phase 1 · Coverage

Every line your tests execute is a line the core can warn you about.

Deprecations are raised at runtime. Removed API fails at runtime. A line of code no test ever executes is a line no tool can warn you about — until an editor executes it in production.

This is why coverage is not a code-quality nicety during an upgrade. It is the difference between finding things in week one and finding them on the night.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk45 / 88

Phase 1 · Coverage

Reading the code vs running it

Static analysis — reads

  • Extension Scanner, Rector, Fractor, PHPStan
  • Limited to a fixed list of known patterns
  • Cannot resolve dynamic calls or string class names
  • Never sees your TCA, TypoScript or data as the core sees them
  • Fast, cheap, runs on every commit

Tests — run

  • The real core, the real bootstrap, a real database
  • Whatever your code actually does, including the dynamic parts
  • Catches changed defaults and changed rendering
  • Reports the core's own deprecation text, verbatim
  • Slower, and the only layer that executes anything

You need both. Static analysis narrows the search; tests prove the result.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk46 / 88

Phase 1 · Coverage

Cover what touches the core

Services and repositories

Anything calling QueryBuilder, FAL, links, language or context. This is where removed API hides.

Plugins and controllers

One functional request per plugin. Registration, routing and TypoScript all change between majors — and a plugin that stops rendering is silent.

ViewHelpers and templates

Fluid changes quietly. A render test costs minutes and catches silent output changes.

Event listeners, hooks and middleware

Registration APIs move. A test proves yours is still called at all.

TCA and FlexForms

A test that only boots is already enough — the core reports its own migrations for you.

Commands and scheduler tasks

Nobody clicks these during a smoke test. They break in the night, unattended.

Rule of thumb: if it calls TYPO3 API, one functional test that executes it pays for itself at every single upgrade — forever.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk47 / 88

Phase 1 · Coverage

What each kind of problem looks like in a test run

Breaking change

  • The API is gone — the code cannot run at all
  • PHPUnit reports an ERROR, with file and line
  • Call to undefined method QueryBuilder::execute()
  • Urgency: now. It cannot run on the new version.

Deprecation

  • Still works — the core raises E_USER_DEPRECATED
  • failOnDeprecation turns it into a build failure
  • The message contains the migration instruction
  • Urgency: before the next major. On your schedule.

One test run separates “must fix to boot” from “must fix before the next flight” — and hands you the migration text for both.

Write the QRH

Phase 1

The departure briefing

  • Say the plan out loud to the people who will fly it with you.
  • Who runs which step, in which order, and who watches what.
  • What going wrong looks like — concretely, not as a feeling.
  • Who is reachable, and who is explicitly not on duty.

A shared mental map is the reason two pilots are better than one. Two people with different plans are worse than one person with a plan.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk50 / 88

Phase 1

Go / No-Go

GO

  • Strong matches at zero, or on the MEL with a date
  • All third-party extensions resolved
  • Backup restored successfully at least once
  • Rollback criteria written and understood
  • The window is long enough for the plan plus surprises

NO-GO

  • “We will find out during the upgrade”
  • An unowned extension nobody can update
  • A backup that has never been restored
  • A window that fits only the happy path
  • The person who knows the system is on holiday

No-Go is a valid, professional outcome. Delaying a flight costs money. The alternative costs more.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk51 / 88
2

The upgrade window itself

Take-Off & Cruise

Now you fly the plan you wrote. You do not write a new one.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk52 / 88

Phase 2

Sterile cockpit

  • Below 10,000 feet, crews may only discuss what is necessary for the flight.
  • No small talk, no paperwork, no non-essential radio calls. It is a rule, not a mood.
  • Your equivalent: content freeze, code freeze, deploy freeze — announced in advance.
  • “While you are in there anyway, could you also…” — no. That is a separate flight.

Most upgrade disasters are not caused by the upgrade. They are caused by the third thing someone did during it.

Phase 2

The order is not a preference

Do these in this order, or do them twice

1Branchgit checkout -b upgrade/v13 — everything after this is reversible
2PlatformPHP version, composer config platform.php, extension constraints
3Packagescomposer update -W — the core and all extensions move together
4RectorNow the new rule sets and the new code are both on disk
5FractorTypoScript, Fluid, YAML — the half Rector never sees
6ScanExtension Scanner AND the TCA migration check — both now carry the target rules
7Schemaextension:setup and the database compare — the point of no return
8Wizardsupgrade:list, then upgrade:run — repeatable, scriptable
9Cachesflush, warm, and only then look at the site

Steps 4 and 5 run AFTER step 3 — that is the one everybody gets wrong.

Phase 2

Rector before the package upgrade refactors against the old world.

The rule sets ship with the tool. The code they must match ships with the new core. You need both on disk before you let anything rewrite your files.

Same for Fractor. Bump first, refactor second, review always.

Phase 2 · Tooling

Rector is a co-pilot, not an autopilot

  • Read every hunk. It rewrote your code — you are still the one who signs for it.
  • Commit in slices, one rule set at a time, so a bad change is one revert and not an archaeological dig.
  • It produces unformatted output — run your CGL fixer afterwards.
  • Never on production. Never outside version control. The tool's own docs say so.

A co-pilot flies the aircraft. A co-pilot does not get to decide where you are going.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk60 / 88

Phase 2 · Tooling

The fix that broke the plugin

Rector migrated the plugin registration. Correctly. And the site went blank.

What Rector did

  • Moved the plugin from a list_type subtype to a real CType
  • Exactly what TYPO3 v13 asks you to do
  • And it scaffolded the upgrade wizard for the data migration
  • …with a // TODO: Add this mapping yourself! left in it

What nobody was told

  • Every existing tt_content row still says CType=list
  • The plugin now matches nothing and renders nothing
  • No error, no log entry, no scanner finding
  • An editor reports it three weeks later

Code migration and data migration are two different jobs. Refactoring tools do the first one and, at best, hand you a stub for the second.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk61 / 88

Phase 2 · Coverage

One test noticed. It was the one that renders the plugin.

TypoScript object path “tt_content.list.20.flightops_board” does not exist. Not a deprecation, not a scanner match, not a Rector diff — a failing assertion in the only test that executes the whole chain.

This is why “cover your plugins” is on the pre-flight checklist. A unit test on the service would have stayed green all the way to production.

What a breaking change looks like

  • File, line, and the exact method. No bisecting, no guessing, no clicking.

Phase 2 · Coverage

Deprecation on Monday. Fatal error on Tuesday. Same test, same line.

On 12.4 that suite reported 4 deprecations and passed every assertion. On 13.4 the same suite reports 6 errors. Nothing about the code changed — only the core underneath it.

This is the whole talk in one command. Your tests are where “today's deprecation is tomorrow's breaking change” stops being a slogan and becomes a line number.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk66 / 88

Phase 2 · Coverage

Working the failures

  • Errors first: a removed API means the code cannot even run. That is your blocking set.
  • Deprecations second: they still work, so they are scheduled work, not emergency work.
  • One fix, one run, one commit — so a wrong fix is one revert, not an investigation.
  • A failure you cannot explain is a changelog you have not read yet.

The suite also tells you when to stop. “Green” is a fact. “I think it works now” is not.

Phase 2 · Tooling

Upgrade wizards

Admin Tools › Upgrade › Upgrade Wizard — TYPO3 13.4.34

  • Wizards migrate DATA and CONFIGURATION — the part no refactoring tool can touch.
  • Schema first: missing tables and fields must exist before any wizard may run.
  • A wizard only appears when it actually has something to migrate — an empty list is an answer.
  • “Mark undone” resets the flag, so a wizard can be re-run on the next environment.

This is also why you rehearse on a copy of production data. On an empty database every wizard looks finished.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk70 / 88

Phase 2 · Tooling

Make it repeatable

Anything you do by hand once, you will do wrong the second time

# Schema first: creates and alters, never drops
./vendor/bin/typo3 extension:setup
./vendor/bin/typo3 cache:flush

# What is waiting, and what already ran?
./vendor/bin/typo3 upgrade:list
./vendor/bin/typo3 upgrade:list --all

# Run one, or run them all - scriptable, repeatable, reviewable
./vendor/bin/typo3 upgrade:run pagesRecyclerDoktypeMigration
./vendor/bin/typo3 upgrade:run
  • The same script runs on your machine, on staging, and in production.
  • That is how the production run stops being the first run.
  • database:updateschema is TYPO3 Console, not core. Drops and renames: Analyze Database Structure.

Phase 2

When it breaks: Aviate · Navigate · Communicate

step 1

Aviate

Keep the system in a known state. Stop changing things. Do not panic-edit production. The aircraft is still flying.

step 2

Navigate

Find out where you actually are. Which step? What does the log say? Is this in your QRH? Read the actual error, not the summary.

step 3

Communicate

Team, community, Slack, documentation, the changelog. Asking for help early is a procedure, not a confession.

The order matters. People who communicate before they aviate crash while typing.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk72 / 88

Phase 2

Two kinds of error

You predicted this one

  • It is in your QRH with a prepared response
  • The changelog entry is already open in a tab
  • You apply the migration and continue
  • Elapsed time: minutes. Stress: low.

You did not

  • Stay calm — this is normal, not a failure
  • Re-read the changelogs; you probably skipped one
  • Check the extension's own upgrade instructions
  • Ask. Then write it into the QRH for next time.

Preparation does not remove surprises. It shrinks the set of them, and it buys you the calm to handle what is left.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk73 / 88

Phase 2

The go-around

  • If the approach is not stable, you go around. Every time. It is not a failure — it is a manoeuvre.
  • Pilots practise go-arounds. The decision is pre-briefed, so it costs nothing to make.
  • Your rollback criteria were written in phase 1, when you were calm and nobody was watching.
  • Execute them without ego. “We are already three hours in” is not a rollback criterion.

The reason to define abort criteria before departure is that you are the worst possible judge of them at 02:00 with a broken site.

The flight does not end at touchdown. It ends at the gate, with the paperwork done.

Phase 3 · Coverage

Green again is not the end of the work. It is the end of the guessing.

A green pipeline on the new version means every path your tests cover behaves. It says nothing about the paths they do not cover — so the smoke test still happens, by a human, on purpose.

And the honest measurement for next time: which failures did your tests catch, and which did a person find afterwards? That gap is your coverage backlog.

Phase 3

Smoke-test the whole aircraft

  • Frontend: every page type, every plugin, every language, images, forms, search.
  • Backend: the tasks your editors actually perform — not the ones you find interesting.
  • The boring infrastructure: mail, redirects, scheduler, indexing, caches, CDN.
  • Have a person who did not do the upgrade click through it. They see what you cannot.

Your test suite proves the code runs. A human proves the site works.

Phase 3 · Tooling

TCA after landing

New migrations arrived

  • The new core added migrations your old core never had
  • Run Check TCA Migrations again — the list is not the one you cleared
  • Every new entry is a fresh deprecation you just inherited

Old migrations left

  • A migration you were silently relying on may be gone
  • Then it is not a deprecation any more — the config is simply ignored
  • Nothing errors. The field just renders wrong, or not at all

This is the half that bites without a stack trace: the autopilot was removed, and the aircraft is quietly out of trim. Only the checklist catches it.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk80 / 88

Phase 3 · Tooling

The deprecation log is your tech log

Pilots write up every defect after the flight, even the small ones

# config/system/additional.php - switch it on, then actually read it
$GLOBALS['TYPO3_CONF_VARS']['LOG']['TYPO3']['CMS']['deprecations']['writerConfiguration'] = [
    \Psr\Log\LogLevel::NOTICE => [
        \TYPO3\CMS\Core\Log\Writer\FileWriter::class => [
            'disabled' => false,
        ],
    ],
];

# then, after a day of real traffic and real editing:
tail -f var/log/typo3_deprecations_*.log
  • Static analysis reads code paths. The deprecation log reports the ones actually taken.
  • It catches the dynamic calls the Extension Scanner structurally cannot see.
  • Let it run under real editor traffic for a few days. That is where the rest hides.

Phase 3

Scan again. You are not finished — you are at the start of the next one.

The version you just landed on deprecates things too. That list is not a leftover. It is the flight plan for the next upgrade, handed to you for free.

Run it now, while the context is still in your head, and put the findings in the backlog with the changelog links attached.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk82 / 88

Phase 3

Remove the ferry equipment

  • Compatibility shims and polyfills you added “just for the migration”.
  • Upgrade-only dev packages — or move them into an isolated tools/ install.
  • The @todo v13 comments you actually resolved. Delete them; do not let them rot.
  • Version constraints still pointing at the old world in your own extensions.

An aircraft flies home with the ferry tank still fitted exactly once. After that it is just weight you pay for on every leg.

Fly the Upgrade — Stefan Bürk83 / 88

Phase 3

The debrief

  • What did we predict correctly? Keep it in the checklist — it earned its place.
  • What surprised us? That is a new QRH entry, written now, not “soon”.
  • What took longest? That is where next time's preparation goes.
  • What did we not need? Delete it. Checklists that grow forever stop being read.

Aviation improves because every incident is written down and shared, not because the next crew is more careful.

Debrief

Takeaways

1
Expect work
An upgrade is a project with phases, not a ticket with an estimate.
2
Expect errors — and prepare for them
You cannot prevent all of them. You can decide in advance how you will react.
3
Read the changelogs
They are your NOTAMs, and every entry already contains its own migration.
4
Check deprecations in all three phases
Today's deprecation is tomorrow's breaking change. Always.
5
Layer your tools
Scanner, Rector, Fractor, the TCA migration check, tests, the deprecation log. Every one has a blind spot the next one covers.
6
Write it down and share it
A plan in one person's head is not a plan. It is a single point of failure.
7
Stay calm
Aviate, navigate, communicate — in that order.
